summary: A granite lighthouse built from the seabed in the tide-race off Fishers Island over seven years, first lit 1 January 1879 and now owned by the New London Maritime Society.

lens.where: replaced by a solar-powered rotating beacon after automation

access.note: Offshore; reachable only by boat. The New London Maritime Society ran limited guided excursions on 26 August 2026; no regular public access.

Iron day-beacon completed; thrown down in 1863
Foundation work begins (April 1871) under Francis Hopkinson Smith; riprap base completed November 1871

November storm damages the station boat beyond use

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The record shows 1878 and 1879. The Light-House Board (1889) and the New London Maritime Society say the lantern was first lit on the night of 1 January 1879; the work was finished in 1878, and USLHS gives 1878 as the establishment year.
LighthouseFriends dates the start of foundation work to April 1871; Johnson (1889) says the work was commenced in 1872. The story states both.

notes_for_editor: Sources: no NRHP text (the PDF is a not-digitised placeholder), and the corpus holds no Light-House Board reports before 1891, so the 1852-1878 construction chronology (appropriations, Smith's work, the riprap failure) rests on LighthouseFriends, which summarises the Board's reports; worth checking against the 1871-1878 reports if time allows. The 1908 Blish/Hansen rescue is likewise LighthouseFriends only (the March 1908 date is not confirmed elsewhere). The Johnson 1889 pier dimensions (67 ft base, 65 ft coping, one-and-a-half-story dwelling) differ from LighthouseFriends (57 ft, 55 ft, two stories); Johnson's OCR may misread 57 as 67, and the story states both. The Willboro grounding and the claim of no loss of life near the light come from a New London Maritime Society exhibit. The Maritime Society's story of a keeper Carroll lost in January 1885 conflicts with the USLHS roster (Thomas S. Carroll, 1882-86); the story reports both without reconciling. The 1931 Bulletin barge name is garbled in OCR (V'iotorioU8); the story says only 'a barge' and does not date the gale. The 1938 Bulletin passage is in two interleaved columns; the Race Rock line was matched by reading across the lines, and the claim is that Race Rock was among the Long Island Sound stations 'principally damaged' by the hurricane. The 1936 ice report is quoted from LighthouseFriends; the original Bulletin item was not found in the corpus text. The NPGallery record gives 'Date Published 4/29/2005', which matches the listing date reported elsewhere but is not stated there as the listing date. Fog-signal hours: both the FY1900 and FY1901 reports give 509 hours, possibly a repeated figure. The 1918 riprap estimate's report year is inferred from the volume's labelling (scan p.378, printed p.64). Fiscal years: the 1896 entries are in the FY ended June 1896 report; the siren, established 20 October 1896, is in the FY1897 report. Roster stints in 1911-1913 and the Coast Guard lines are as printed by USLHS; roles for Coast Guard personnel are 'other' because the archive gives no position. Culver's age (24 in 1892) is from the newspaper only. Lens: the original fourth-order lens's current whereabouts is unknown; the record's range (14 nm) and tower height (14 m) were not confirmed by a source read and are omitted. Fact-check 2026-10-22: story now states the 1871 (LighthouseFriends) vs 1872 (Johnson) start; NRHP date is the NPS record date, not a stated listing date; the Maritime Society's 'no shipwrecks' claim is set beside the 1908 Volund report.
